content: Analysis is essential to evaluate the effectiveness of treatment methods in removing contaminants. Cyanobacteria, which are associated with the production of cyanotoxins, have been extensively studied. Bernard et al. (2016) provided insights into this topic, and further information can be found in the Handbook of Cyanobacterial Monitoring and Cyanotoxin Analysis edited by Meriluoto, Spoof, and Codd (2017). Additionally, the second edition of Toxic Cyanobacteria in Water, edited by Chorus and Welker, published by CRC Press on behalf of the World Health Organization (WHO), offers comprehensive guidance on this subject. Guideline values (GVs) and provisional guideline values (pGVs) are critical for assessing short-term and acute exposure risks. For example, AL2 values are used for short-term provisional reference values, while AL1 thresholds for anatoxins (ATXs) and saxitoxins (STXs) are not formal WHO values for lifetime exposure but are set at concentrations tenfold lower than those for acute exposure. Detailed interpretation of these values can be found in Chapter 12 of the WHO guidelines. Indicator organisms serve various purposes, such as monitoring fecal pollution, validating the effectiveness of filtration or disinfection processes, and assessing the integrity and cleanliness of water distribution systems. Total coliform bacteria, a group of aerobic and facultatively anaerobic, Gram-negative, non-spore-forming bacilli, are capable of fermenting lactose and producing acid or aldehyde within 24 hours at 35–37°C. Escherichia coli (E. coli) and thermotolerant coliforms are subsets of this group, with E. coli being a reliable indicator of fecal contamination. However, total coliforms are less useful as indicators of fecal pathogens but can help assess the cleanliness of distribution systems and the potential presence of biofilms. E. coli is present in high numbers in human and animal feces and is rarely found in the absence of fecal pollution. It is considered the most suitable indicator of fecal contamination. Thermotolerant coliforms, which include some environmental organisms, are less reliable but acceptable indicators. E. coli is also used in monitoring programs for drinking-water quality verification and as a disinfection indicator, although direct measurement of disinfectant residuals is faster and more reliable. Heterotrophic plate counts (HPC) detect a wide range of heterotrophic microorganisms, including bacteria and fungi, based on their ability to grow on rich media under specified conditions. HPC organisms include those sensitive to disinfection, such as coliform bacteria, and those resistant to disinfection, such as spore formers. While HPC tests are not direct indicators of pathogen presence, they are useful for operational monitoring, assessing treatment and disinfection effectiveness, and evaluating the cleanliness and integrity of distribution systems. HPC organisms can proliferate in treated water in the absence of residual disinfectants and form biofilms on surfaces in contact with water. Intestinal enterococci, a subgroup of fecal streptococci, are Gram-positive bacteria that are relatively tolerant of sodium chloride and alkaline pH levels. They are facultatively anaerobic and occur singly, in pairs, or as short chains. This group includes species such as Enterococcus faecalis, E. faecium, E. durans, and E. hirae, which are relatively specific indicators of fecal pollution. Most species do not multiply in water environments, making them reliable indicators of fecal contamination. Their numbers in human feces are generally about an order of magnitude lower than those of E. coli. In summary, the presence of indicator organisms such as E. coli, thermotolerant coliforms, and intestinal enterococci in water provides evidence of fecal contamination and highlights potential issues with treatment processes or distribution system integrity. These organisms are critical for monitoring water quality and ensuring public health safety.
